title: Introduction to Physiotherapy
description: The physiotherapy profession, movement science basics, assessment principles, therapeutic modalities and professional practice in Nigeria.

topics.title: The Physiotherapy Profession
topics.summary: Definition, history, scope of practice, specialties and regulation in Nigeria.

notes.b: Physiotherapy (physical therapy) develops, maintains and restores maximum movement and functional ability throughout life, using physical approaches: exercise, manual therapy, electrophysical agents, education and advice. Specialties include musculoskeletal and sports, neurological, cardiopulmonary, paediatric, women's health, geriatric and community-based rehabilitation. Physiotherapists work within the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), which considers body functions and structures, activities and participation, and environmental and personal factors.
k: ICF: impairment, activity limitation, participation restriction

notes.b: In Nigeria physiotherapists are registered by the Medical Rehabilitation Therapists (Registration) Board of Nigeria (MRTB), and the professional association is the Nigeria Society of Physiotherapy (NSP, founded 1959). The World Physiotherapy (formerly WCPT) is the global body; World Physiotherapy Day is 8 September. Nigerian university programmes (e.g. at the University of Ibadan, University of Lagos, OAU, University of Nigeria, Bayero University) award BMR(PT) or BPT/DPT degrees after five years including clinical internship.

topics.title: Basic Movement Science and Terminology
topics.summary: Planes and axes of movement, joint movements, and types of muscle contraction.

notes.b: Movements occur in planes around axes: flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane around a frontal (coronal) axis; abduction and adduction in the frontal plane around a sagittal axis; rotation in the transverse plane around a vertical axis. Other terms: circumduction, pronation/supination (forearm), inversion/eversion (foot), dorsiflexion/plantarflexion (ankle), protraction/retraction, elevation/depression (scapula). Range of motion (ROM) is measured with a goniometer; normal knee flexion is about 0–135/140°.

Isometric contraction produces tension without change in muscle length (e.g. static quadriceps exercise). Isotonic contraction changes length: concentric (muscle shortens — lifting a weight) and eccentric (muscle lengthens under load — lowering a weight; generates more force and more delayed-onset soreness). Isokinetic contraction occurs at a constant speed on special equipment. Muscles act as agonists (prime movers), antagonists (oppose), synergists and fixators (stabilisers). Levers: first class (neck extension), second class (standing on tiptoes), third class (most common — biceps flexing the elbow).

topics.title: Physiotherapy Assessment
topics.summary: Subjective and objective assessment, muscle power grading, pain measurement and outcome measures.

notes.b: Assessment begins with the subjective examination: presenting complaint, history, pain (site, nature, severity, aggravating/easing factors, 24-hour pattern), past medical history, social history and patient goals; 'red flags' (e.g. unexplained weight loss, night pain, bladder or bowel dysfunction with back pain suggesting cauda equina syndrome) need urgent medical referral. The objective examination includes observation, palpation, range of motion, muscle power, special tests, neurological examination, balance and functional assessment. Findings are summarised into a problem list and SMART goals.
k: Cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel change

notes.b: Muscle power is graded with the Oxford (MRC) scale 0–5: 0 no contraction; 1 flicker; 2 movement with gravity eliminated; 3 movement against gravity; 4 against some resistance; 5 normal power. Pain is measured on a visual analogue scale (VAS, 0–100 mm) or numerical rating scale (0–10). Spasticity is graded by the Modified Ashworth Scale. Common outcome measures: Timed Up and Go test (falls risk), Berg Balance Scale, Barthel Index (activities of daily living), 6-minute walk test (endurance).

topics.title: Therapeutic Modalities
topics.summary: Heat and cold, electrotherapy, ultrasound and exercise therapy basics.

notes.b: Superficial heat (hot packs, infrared, paraffin wax) increases blood flow, reduces pain and muscle spasm, and increases tissue extensibility before stretching; it is contraindicated in acute inflammation, impaired sensation, bleeding disorders and over malignancy. Cryotherapy (ice packs) is used in acute soft tissue injuries to reduce pain, swelling and metabolic rate — the PRICE principle (Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation), now often POLICE (Protection, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation). Apply ice for about 10–20 minutes with a barrier to avoid ice burns.
k: Heat before stretching; not in acute inflammation
Ice for acute injury, 10–20 min with a barrier

notes.b: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) relieves pain via the pain gate theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) and endogenous opioid release. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) produces muscle contraction to strengthen weak muscles. Therapeutic ultrasound (1 MHz for deeper, 3 MHz for superficial tissues) has thermal and non-thermal effects; avoid over the eyes, gravid uterus, malignancy and pacemakers. Exercise therapy includes passive, active-assisted, active and resisted exercises, stretching, strengthening, balance and aerobic training — the cornerstone of physiotherapy.
k: Exercise is the cornerstone of physiotherapy

topics.title: Disability, Rehabilitation and Assistive Devices
topics.summary: Models of disability, rehabilitation team, walking aids and community-based rehabilitation.

notes.b: The medical model sees disability as a problem of the individual's body to be cured; the social model sees disability as created by barriers in society (attitudes, buildings, transport). The biopsychosocial model (underlying ICF) combines both. Rehabilitation is a team effort: physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech and language therapists, prosthetists/orthotists, doctors, nurses, psychologists and social workers. In Nigeria the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 protects the rights of persons with disabilities. Community-based rehabilitation (CBR), promoted by WHO, brings services to communities using local resources.
k: Medical vs social model; biopsychosocial model

notes.b: Walking aids increase the base of support and reduce weight-bearing on an injured limb. Walking frames give the most stability; axillary crutches allow non-weight-bearing; elbow crutches are used for longer-term use; walking sticks give least support. A walking stick is held in the hand opposite the affected leg and moved together with it. Crutch gait patterns: non-weight-bearing (three-point swing-through), partial weight-bearing, and four-point gait. The correct height of a stick is at the level of the ulnar styloid/greater trochanter with the elbow flexed about 15–20°. On stairs: 'up with the good, down with the bad'.
k: Stick in the hand opposite the affected leg
Stairs: up with the good, down with the bad
